To: t-achilles
Replying to: p04
Cc: none
Subject: none

Hi Mel — the jump in k’s, morning stiffness, and tenderness and thickening a few centimetres above the heel can fit a load-related mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy. That’s more typical than an acute tear with no sudden incident, but I haven’t assessed your leg, so this is general guidance rather than a diagnosis.

Complete rest usually isn’t needed, but pushing on unchanged isn’t the aim either. Since you were limping after the 6k, that was too much for now. Reduce the distance and park the hills, sprints and speedwork. Keep running and strengthening pain to about 3/10 or less, without it building as you go, and it should be back to its previous level by the next morning. If morning pain or stiffness is increasing, reduce the load again.

Heel drops are one option, but heavy, slow calf strengthening has better evidence these days. A reasonable starting point is straight-knee and bent-knee calf raises, slowly up and down, for 3 sets of 8–12, three times a week. Start with two legs or bodyweight if needed, then progress to single-leg raises and gradually add weight so the final reps are genuinely challenging. On grumpy days, comfortable isometric calf holds — roughly 5 holds of 30–45 seconds — can be a better option than forcing painful reps.

I wouldn’t stretch it aggressively until it burns. Cortisone into or close to the Achilles is also generally avoided because of the potential for tendon damage; it isn’t just a quick fix.

Some antibiotics, particularly fluoroquinolones, can increase the risk of tendon problems. If you’ve recently taken any, mention that to your GP or physio, and don’t stop a prescribed course without medical advice.

If it isn’t clearly settling over the next 3–4 weeks, book in with any sports physio near Bayswater — earlier if you can’t find a tolerable level of activity.

One important exception: a sudden pop, feeling like you’ve been kicked in the back of the leg, or being unable to push off means stop running and all calf exercises and get it checked urgently that day, through a GP or ED, so a rupture can be ruled out.
